A Hindu is an adherent of Hinduism, one of the world's oldest and major religions, or someone who identifies with the cultural and philosophical traditions originating on the Indian subcontinent.

Origin of the Term

• Geographical Root: The word comes from the Sanskrit Sindhu (the Indus River). Ancient Persians and Greeks used "Hindu" or indoi to describe the people living across or near the Indus River.
• Religious Definition: Over centuries—particularly by the 19th century under British writers—the term shifted from a geographic label to a designator for the diverse religious and spiritual traditions of India.
• Sanatana Dharma: Many followers prefer the term Sanātana Dharma (meaning the "Eternal Religion" or "Eternal Law").

• No Single Founder: Unlike many global faiths, Hinduism has no single founder, no central governing body, and no single mandatory scripture.
• Diverse Divinity: It accommodates monotheism, polytheism, panthenism, and philosophy. Many practice henotheism (focusing on one supreme reality like Brahman while honoring various forms of gods and goddesses). Key deities include Brahma (the Creator), Vishnu (the Preserver), and Shiva (the Destroyer).
• Fundamental Concepts:
	• Karma: The moral law of cause and effect where actions shape future outcomes.
	• Dharma: Cosmic and social duty, ethics, and righteous living.
	• Samsara & Reincarnation: The cycle of birth, death, and rebirth of the soul (atman).
	• Moksha: Liberation or spiritual freedom from the cycle of rebirth.
